Type.evidence_source: Three major themes from the interviews, identified in at least 85% of the participants' narratives, illuminated the depth of their psychological pain associated with their struggles with mental illness.

Area.evidence_source: The Asian immigrant patients with no history of suicide attempts shared a similar clinical profile with the repeated attempters in terms of nonadherence to treatment and repeated psychiatric hospitalizations (see Table 2). While a higher percentage of the repeated suicide attempters were characterized as having maladaptive personality traits (impulsivity and personality disorder diagnosis, a history of alcohol and substance abuse, family history of suicide attempts, and history of inconsistent utilization of mental health services), chi-square tests yielded no statistical significance in these clinical issues that are generally deemed as suicide risk factors. The only noted significance was the experience of command auditory hallucinations during times of decompensation (52% repeated attempters, 3% nonattempters, p < .001). In the interview sample, five (42%) of the participants also reported hearing voices that urged them to kill themselves preceding one or more of their attempts. While persisting symptoms of mental illness, especially command auditory hallucinations, could increase patients' risks of suicidal ideation and behavior, interviews with persons who made repeated attempts indicated that the psychological and social impact of suffering from a mental illness was a more pervasive factor exacerbating their feelings of helplessness and hopelessness.
